name: builder
intent: Separate a stepwise construction algorithm from a product's representation while giving callers named, order-independent configuration for many optional values; use the same builder protocol for alternate products only when their construction steps genuinely align.
problem: An object with many optional values or ordered parts makes telescoping constructors unreadable: identically typed positional arguments can be silently swapped, while setter-based assembly exposes half-initialised state and scatters cross-field validation instead of giving one terminal construction boundary.
context: Use when construction has a meaningful sequence of parts (documents, messages, queries, trees or test fixtures), many optional settings with defaults, cross-field rules that must hold before publication, or one recipe that should drive multiple representations; distinguish that from a plain data aggregate that named/default arguments or a record can construct directly.
benefits: Callers pass only what they care about and name every value, so the call site reads as configuration instead of as a parameter count.
The product is constructed once, at the end: a half-initialised object is never visible and cross-field invariants have a single place to be enforced (build()).

The same step sequence can be driven over different builders - or pre-recorded in a Director - so one construction algorithm yields different representations (GoF's RTF readers producing ASCII, TeX or a widget tree).
Adding an optional setting is additive: a new step does not break existing call sites, which positional constructors cannot promise.
The product can be immutable: the builder absorbs the mutability while it accumulates and build() hands out a value that is safe to share.
tradeoffs: The builder duplicates the product's field list, so a new field must be added in two places and the compiler will not flag the omission (generated builders exist precisely to remove this).
The builder is mutable scratch state: it cannot be shared between threads, and reusing one instance - or branching from a stored one - silently mixes configurations.

Validation concentrates in the terminal step, so an invalid value surfaces late unless every step validates eagerly, and a builder with no validation simply postpones the telescoping-constructor mistakes to runtime.
Requiredness is no longer checked by the compiler: a hand-written builder that starts empty can be built incomplete, which is why staged/type-safe builders exist.

Each construction costs an extra object plus a copy of the accumulated state, and the product must be made immutable deliberately: a build() that hands out the builder's own collections aliases mutable state.
The indirection spreads over more types (builder, product, sometimes Director and a builder interface), which for a small object costs more code than the constructor it replaces.

participants.responsibility: Declares the step methods that configure a product and holds the accumulated values and defaults until construction finishes; in the modern optional-parameter form it also owns the validation.

Implements the steps for one concrete representation, keeps track of the representation it is building and exposes the operation that returns it (Build(), getResult()). In the fluent form the Builder and ConcreteBuilder roles merge into a single class.

Runs a fixed sequence of steps against a Builder so one construction recipe can be reused with different builders; optional - the client can drive the steps directly, and in the fluent form the Director is usually dropped.
The complex object under construction; it is only published after the steps have finished and is typically immutable from then on.
Creates and configures the builder (or registers it with a Director) and retrieves the finished product from the builder.

use_cases: Configuration objects assembled from defaults plus overrides coming from a file, environment variables and command-line flags, where most settings stay untouched.

Requests, messages and jobs with optional headers, timeouts, retries and credentials (OkHttp's Request.Builder, ASP.NET Core's HostApplicationBuilder, protobuf-generated message APIs and Lombok @Builder).
Query construction where clauses are added as data arrives (Knex, TypeORM's SelectQueryBuilder, SQLAlchemy Core's select().where()).
Documents and reports where one parse-and-build algorithm must produce several representations (GoF's RTF reader emitting ASCII, TeX or a widget tree).

Test data built from a named set of valid defaults that each test tweaks (test data builders / object mothers); isolated setup where adding one field to the domain model requires only updating the builder, not every test.
Immutable domain values with many fields that must be created through a private constructor and validated as a whole.

DSL and fluent-API construction for internal languages (Kotlin type-safe builders, Ktor routing DSLs, jQuery-style chains, SQL query builders): the builder encodes grammar rules so illegal states cannot be expressed.
Complex object graphs where nested sub-objects each have their own builders (a OrderBuilder containing ItemBuilder references), with collection add() and addAll() steps for aggregates.
API client objects where headers, timeouts, base URLs and credentials are accumulated before a single build() call that constructs an immutable, ready-to-share client.
Test doubles and mock configuration (Mockito MockSettings, WireMock StubBuilder) where builder steps configure behaviour and build() returns an immutable mock with no further mutation allowed.

Generated construction APIs such as Protocol Buffers field setters and Lombok @Builder, where generation removes hand-written field plumbing but domain validation still belongs at the construction boundary.

Incremental text assembly with java.lang.StringBuilder (append/insert followed by toString()) is a builder-shaped accumulator, not a GoF multi-representation Builder; use it when the product is simply a string.

Per-request HTTP construction where the fluent builder is documented as not thread-safe and build() may be called repeatedly, each call producing a fresh immutable request from the builder's current state (java.net.http.HttpRequest.Builder).

Subprocess assembly where one configured attribute set — command, working directory, environment, redirects — launches several processes and the terminal operation is start() rather than build() (java.lang.ProcessBuilder, startPipeline).

Generative query building where each chained step returns a new statement object instead of mutating the builder, so a partially built query can be safely shared and branched (SQLAlchemy 2.x select().where().join()).
avoid_when: The object has fewer than about four fields and no optional ones: a constructor, a record/struct literal or an aggregate initializer is shorter and needs no second type.

The language names arguments and applies defaults at the call site (Kotlin, Python, Swift, Scala, Ruby, C# object initializers, Java records): use the language, and reach for a builder only for staged or validated construction.
Settings are purely optional with sensible defaults and no cross-field rules: functional options (Go) or an options object with defaults is lighter.
The object is created once, never varied and has no invariants: a named constructor or static factory reads better than a builder chain.
A copy of an already configured instance is required: prototype-style copy-with (with, copy(), clone) is one call instead of rebuilding.

The only operation is appending text or bytes and there is no domain validation or alternate representation: use StringBuilder or the standard byte accumulator directly instead of inventing field setters.
anti_patterns: God builder: mirror every field of a large object -> a second unvalidated model drifts from the product -> split the product or generate the builder from its schema.
Setter bag: builder methods only assign fields and build() does no validation -> JavaBeans mutability is renamed, not solved -> use a constructor/record or enforce invariants at build().
Two-phase initialisation in disguise: build() returns a partially filled object -> callers observe invalid intermediate state -> keep the product private until terminal construction completes.
Reusing or caching one builder instance -> later products share mutable collections or threads interleave calls -> create a fresh builder per product and never publish its scratch state.

Hand-rolled builder chains in a language with named/default parameters or object initializers -> boilerplate duplicates the constructor -> use the native construction form unless staging or validation adds real value.
Speculative builder: add steps for fields that never vary across call sites -> the builder becomes a second source of truth -> expose only decisions that genuinely vary.
Builder that hides a single-responsibility violation: an object needs a builder with 15 steps -> unrelated concerns are coupled behind one API -> split the product into cohesive values.

Long-parameter-list smell disguised: a builder with 20 step methods is a telescoping constructor written vertically -> callers still face one oversized concept -> introduce parameter objects or smaller products.

Hierarchical builder without self-type: subclass methods return the parent type -> the fluent chain loses subclass operations and needs casts -> use a self-referential generic or covariant return type.

Strict staged-builder API fragility: inserting a required step changes every staged type chain -> source compatibility breaks for existing callers -> reserve staged builders for stable protocols or add new terminal paths.
design_principles: Separate the construction algorithm from the representation of the product, so the two can change independently.
Single responsibility at the construction boundary: the builder only accumulates and validates a valid configuration.
Fail fast on the whole object: check invariant-spanning rules once, on the copied fields, in the step that constructs the product.
Immutability by default: hide the product's constructor and hand out an immutable value so it can be shared safely.
Open/closed: optional steps are added without touching existing call sites, while required values stay in the constructor.
best_practices: Make the builder the only way to construct the product (private or package-private constructor, or build() as the single public factory) and validate in build().
Copy collections and freeze the product in build(); never hand the builder's own mutable fields to the product.
Name steps after the domain decision they represent (withTimeout, forUser, addHeader) rather than after the field they assign.
Keep the builder mutable and single-use: create a fresh one per product, or offer copy-on-write builders if reuse is a real requirement.
If steps must happen in order, use a staged/type-safe builder (one type per step) instead of runtime checks inside build().
Use a Director or a factory function for construction recipes that repeat in more than one place, so the sequence is written once.
Put required values in the builder's constructor or static factory method, not in optional steps, so the compiler enforces completeness.
Validate eagerly at each step when the invariant is local to that step; defer cross-field validation to build().
For builder hierarchies (subclass returns self-type), use a self-referential generic (GenericBuilder<Self>) so the compiler catches missing return-type overrides.
In test data builders: provide sensible defaults for every field so any test can build() without specifying everything, but pass every value the test actually asserts.
Avoid speculative builders: only add steps for fields that genuinely vary across call sites — a builder that mirrors every field of a large object is a God builder smell.

When the language supports it (Kotlin, Scala), prefer native type-safe builders and DSL constructs over hand-rolled fluent chains; fall back to hand-written builders only when staged validation is required.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Builder (Creational Patterns): intent, participants, consequences and the RTF reader example.

related_patterns_notes.type-safe-builder: Encodes required steps and ordering in types; choose it when compile-time completeness matters, while an ordinary builder may validate only at runtime.
related_patterns_notes.functional-options: Configures one product through composable functions rather than a mutable builder; prefer it in Go for optional settings without a staged chain.
related_patterns_notes.fluent-interface: Describes a chaining API independently of construction; a builder may use fluent methods to accumulate state before build().
related_patterns_notes.named-constructor: Exposes a small set of semantic creation paths; use it instead of a builder when variants are few and fixed.
related_patterns_notes.abstract-factory: Creates families of related products; Builder controls ordered assembly of one product or representation.
related_patterns_notes.factory-method: Delegates which concrete product to instantiate; Builder separates stepwise assembly from the final representation.
related_patterns_notes.parameter-object: Groups arguments into a value; Builder is useful when that value must be assembled incrementally or validated across steps.
related_patterns_notes.composite: Models recursive part-whole treatment; Builder may assemble the tree but does not define uniform operations over it.
related_patterns_notes.test-data-builder: Specializes Builder with valid defaults and explicit fixture overrides; it is not a production Director or domain factory.
related_patterns_notes.object-mother: Returns predefined fixtures, while a test-data builder composes adjustable variations without a growing factory-method list.
